conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor seeing you tonight. I understand you’ve had abdominal pain around your G-tube site—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three days ago I stepped on the tube at home and it yanked hard. I’ve had pain since, and it’s been leaking more. The skin looks red too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea? Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting or diarrhea. I don’t think I’ve had a fever. I’m mostly worried I pulled it out of place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. On exam your belly is soft and only minimally tender right around the tube, and I don’t feel signs of a severe abdominal infection. The redness is in a very square shape where the bandage sits, which can happen from irritation and moisture under the dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The drainage is yellow and kind of cloudy. Is that pus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now it doesn’t smell bad and the skin isn’t hot or hard, which is reassuring. Sometimes tube feed can leak around the site and look yellow and cloudy. But because you had a strong tug and ongoing pain, we want to make sure the tube is still in the stomach and there’s no leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do you check that? I’ve had so many tube problems before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do a G-tube contrast study—radiology injects a small amount of water-soluble contrast through the tube and takes X-rays to confirm it goes into the stomach and small bowel without leaking outside. While we’re waiting, we’ll keep you NPO—no tube feeds—and give IV fluids and pain medicine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no feeds tonight? I’m worried I’ll get low blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep a close eye on you. The IV fluids help, and we’ll restart feeds as soon as the study shows it’s safe. If you feel symptoms of low blood sugar, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is really right at the tube. It stings when anything touches it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see some granulation tissue at the site—that extra healing tissue can be very tender and can ooze. We’ll do more frequent dressing changes to keep it clean and dry, and we can give you medication for pain while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do my labs show infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work looks reassuring—your white blood cell count is normal, and your kidney function is normal. Your urine test is negative as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When is the X-ray study happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been completed. The images show the tube tip is in the stomach. When they put in about 20 mL of contrast, it filled the stomach and moved into the small bowel, and there was no contrast leaking outside. That means no evidence of a perforation or leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it didn’t get pulled out of place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—the tube appears well positioned and patent. The pain is most likely from the tugging injury and the irritated tissue at the skin level, plus the leakage causing skin irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I restart my tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll restart your tube feeds and watch for any nausea, vomiting, worsening pain, or abdominal distension. If you tolerate feeds, that’s another reassuring sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeds are going in okay. The drainage is still there though. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some drainage can persist, especially if there’s leakage around the tube. What we’re watching is whether it becomes foul-smelling, the redness spreads, or you develop fever. With frequent dressing changes, the skin irritation often improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The redness looks better this morning, but it still hurts when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I agree—the redness has nearly resolved compared with last night. The site is still tender where the granulation tissue is. We’ll transition you to oral pain medication as needed and keep focusing on good dressing care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need antibiotics? I’m worried because I’ve had MRSA before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s no sign of a deep infection—no fever, no elevated white count, and the skin findings look like irritation from the dressing and leakage rather than cellulitis. If anything changes—spreading redness, warmth, worsening pain, or fever—you should call right away or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan when I go home? I’m scared it’ll get yanked again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re safe to go home today. Keep doing frequent dressing changes to keep the area clean and dry. Continue your tube feeds as you’ve been doing since you’re tolerating them. We’re sending you with oxycodone for pain as needed and docusate to prevent constipation. And you’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in about two weeks—if the tube keeps bothering you, it may need repositioning in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call urgently if you develop fever, worsening abdominal pain, vomiting, a hard or distended belly, rapidly spreading redness, foul-smelling drainage, or if the tube stops working or gets pulled out. Otherwise, keep up the dressing care and we’ll see you in clinic.
